okunev-culture.name: Okunev culture
okunev-culture.summary: A south Siberian Bronze Age culture of pastoralists in the Minusinsk Basin, dated from the late 3rd to early 2nd millennium BCE, formed from local Neolithic forest cultures with some steppe admixture.

minusinsk-hollow.name: Minusinsk Hollow
minusinsk-hollow.summary: A basin in Khakassia and Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia, situated among the mountains of southern Siberia.

andronovo-culture.name: Andronovo culture
andronovo-culture.summary: A group of related Late Bronze Age cultures from about 2000 to 1150 BCE, spanning from the southern Urals to central Siberia and western Xinjiang, generally agreed to have been Indo-Iranian.

bactria-margiana-archaeological-complex.name: Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex
bactria-margiana-archaeological-complex.summary: A Bronze Age civilisation of southern Central Asia, also called the Oxus Civilization, that flourished between about 2500 and 1700 BCE across sites in Bactria, Margiana and surrounding regions.

altyndepe.name: Altyn-Depe
altyndepe.summary: Bronze Age archaeological site in Turkmenistan, inhabited from about 3200 to 2000 BC, that grew into a full urban settlement by its later period.

begash.name: Begash
begash.summary: An archaeological site in Kazakhstan's Koksu River valley where transhumant herders buried their dead and left the earliest known evidence of domesticated grains in Central Asia.

triticum-turgidum.name: Triticum turgidum
triticum-turgidum.summary: A species of wheat, also known as pasta, macaroni or durum wheat, native to areas around the eastern Mediterranean, Iran and Xinjiang in China.

proso-millet.name: Proso millet
proso-millet.summary: A grain crop first domesticated about 10,000 years ago in Northern China, notable for its very short growing cycle and low water requirements.

tazabagyab-culture.name: Tazabagyab culture
tazabagyab-culture.summary: A late Bronze Age culture, about 1850 to 1500 BC, in the lower Zeravshan valley and lower Amu Darya near the Aral Sea, once considered an offshoot of the Andronovo culture.

karakum-desert.name: Karakum Desert
karakum-desert.summary: The 12th largest desert in the world, covering about 70 percent of Turkmenistan, sparsely populated and receiving very little rainfall.

syr-darya.name: Syr Darya
syr-darya.summary: A 2,256-kilometre river in Central Asia, historically called the Jaxartes, flowing from Kyrgyzstan through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan toward the Aral Sea.

deer-stones-culture.name: Deer stones
deer-stones-culture.summary: Bronze Age megaliths carved with images of flying deer, found mainly in Mongolia and nearby Siberia, generally placed near ancient graves and thought to guard the dead.

scytho-siberian-art.name: Scytho-Siberian art
scytho-siberian-art.summary: Decorative art, especially jewellery, of nomadic Eurasian Steppe peoples from about the 7th to 3rd centuries BC, including the distinctive Animal Style depicting real and fantastical creatures.

scytho-siberian-world.name: Scytho-Siberian world
scytho-siberian-world.summary: An archaeological horizon across the Eurasian Steppe from about the 9th century BC to the 2nd century AD, uniting Scythian, Sarmatian and related Central Asian and Siberian cultures through shared weapons, horse gear and jewellery styles.

saka.name: Saka
saka.summary: Nomadic Eastern Iranian peoples of the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin from the 9th century BC to the 5th century AD, closely related to the Scythians.

tuva.name: Tuva
tuva.summary: A republic of Russia in southern Siberia, at the geographic center of Asia, historically controlled by Chinese dynasties and nomadic khanates before being annexed by the Soviet Union in 1944.

chemurchek-culture.name: Chemurchek culture
chemurchek-culture.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological culture (about 2750 to 1900 BCE) of western Mongolia and nearby Xinjiang and Kazakhstan, known for large rectangular stone-fenced collective tombs, distinct from the earlier Afanasievo culture.

karasuk-culture.name: Karasuk culture
karasuk-culture.summary: A group of late Bronze Age societies, about 1500 to 800 BC, that ranged across Central Asia and southern Siberia from the Aral Sea to the upper Yenisei and Altai Mountains.

shang-dynasty.name: Shang dynasty
shang-dynasty.summary: A Chinese royal dynasty that ruled the Yellow River valley in the 2nd millennium BCE, the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by archaeology, known for oracle-bone writing found at its capital near Anyang.

altai-mountains.name: Altai Mountains
altai-mountains.summary: Mountain range in Central Asia where Russia, China, Mongolia, and Kazakhstan meet, home to a sparse, ethnically diverse population including Turkic peoples and Mongols.

sintashta-culture.name: Sintashta culture
sintashta-culture.summary: A Middle Bronze Age archaeological culture of the Southern Urals (c. 2200–1900 BCE), thought to be the origin of the Indo-Iranian languages and the earliest known chariots, with fortified, militaristic settlements.

seima-turbino-culture.name: Seima-Turbino culture
seima-turbino-culture.summary: A pattern of Bronze Age burial sites across northern Eurasia sharing similar bronze artifacts, linked to nomadic warrior-metalworkers who traveled on horseback or two-wheeled carts, dated to about 2200 to 1900 BCE.

arkaim.name: Arkaim
arkaim.summary: A fortified archaeological site (c. 2150–1650 BC) of the Sintashta culture in Russia's Southern Urals, discovered in 1987 and linked to early Proto-Indo-Iranian speakers.

anyang.name: Anyang
anyang.summary: A city in Henan, China, and site of the ancient capital of Yin, the first stable capital of the Shang dynasty and one of the birthplaces of Chinese civilization.

guifang.name: Guifang
guifang.summary: An ancient northern people who fought the Shang dynasty (1600–1046 BCE); the Chinese name combines words meaning 'ghost' and 'border country.'

sayan-mountains.name: Sayan Mountains
sayan-mountains.summary: Mountain range in southern Siberia, spanning southern Russia and northern Mongolia, that feeds the upper Yenisei River and Lake Baikal. It once marked the border between the Russian Empire and the Qing dynasty.

krotov-culture.name: Krotov culture
krotov-culture.summary: Bronze Age culture of animal breeders, hunters and fishers in the upper Irtysh river basin of Western Siberia, c. 2000–1200 BCE. It marks the first period of developed bronze there, before the Andronovo culture.

kurgan.name: Kurgan
kurgan.summary: A type of burial mound built over a grave, originating on the Pontic–Caspian steppe and spreading through Central Asia and Europe, with the earliest examples dating to the fourth millennium BC.

david-w-anthony.name: David W. Anthony
david-w-anthony.summary: American anthropologist specializing in horse domestication and Indo-European migrations, known for his book The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007).

krivoye-lake.name: Krivoye Lake
krivoye-lake.summary: Small oxbow lake in Russia's Chelyabinsk Oblast, best known for a chariot burial found there dated to around 2000 BC, among the earliest known.

mitanni.name: Mitanni
mitanni.summary: A Hurrian-speaking kingdom in northern Syria and southeast Anatolia, around 1550 to 1260 BCE, a major regional power bordered by the Hittites, Egyptians, Kassites and Assyrians.

proto-indo-iranian-language.name: Proto-Indo-Iranian language
proto-indo-iranian-language.summary: The reconstructed proto-language of the Indo-Iranian branch, spoken in the late 3rd millennium BCE and linked to the Sintashta culture, ancestor of Sanskrit and Avestan.

vedic-sanskrit.name: Vedic Sanskrit
vedic-sanskrit.summary: The earliest attested form of Sanskrit, an Indo-Aryan language found in the Vedas and related texts composed between the mid-2nd and mid-1st millennium BCE, preserved orally before writing existed.

avestan.name: Avestan
avestan.summary: The liturgical language of Zoroastrianism, an Iranian branch of Indo-European spoken from about 1500 to 400 BCE and closely related to Vedic Sanskrit.

gathas.name: Gathas
gathas.summary: The central hymns of Zoroastrianism, traditionally attributed to Zarathustra and composed in the oldest attested Iranian language, among the oldest surviving Indo-European texts.

zoroaster.name: Zoroaster
zoroaster.summary: Iranian religious reformer traditionally dated to the 7th-6th centuries BC (some scholars place him earlier), who became the spiritual founder of Zoroastrianism through his hymns, the Gathas.

avesta.name: Avesta
avesta.summary: The corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, composed orally over centuries before being written down under the Sasanians and later largely lost after the Islamic conquest of Iran.

avestan-alphabet.name: Avestan alphabet
avestan-alphabet.summary: A writing system created during Iran's Sasanian era to render the Avestan language, used to record the Zoroastrian scriptures.

turya-avesta.name: Turya
turya-avesta.summary: A people named in the Avesta, the sacred texts of Zoroastrianism, who closely interacted with the early Iranians; their true identity is unknown, but they are thought to have been Iranic horse nomads from the Eurasian steppe.

turan.name: Turan
turan.summary: A historical region of Central Asia, named for the Tur, an Iranian tribe of the Avestan age; the term can denote a settlement, a geographical area, or a culture.

proto-indo-european-language.name: Proto-Indo-European language
proto-indo-european-language.summary: The reconstructed common ancestor of all Indo-European languages, likely spoken from about 4500 to 2500 BCE, possibly originating in the Pontic-Caspian steppe.

asha.name: Asha
asha.summary: A Zoroastrian concept meaning truth, righteousness and cosmic order, central to Zoroastrian theology and personified as the divinity Asha Vahishta.

ahura-mazda.name: Ahura Mazda
ahura-mazda.summary: The chief god and sky deity of Zoroastrianism, first prominently invoked in the Achaemenid-era Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great.

yasht.name: Yashts
yasht.summary: A Middle Persian term for sacrifice or worship, most often applied to a collection of 21 hymns within the Avesta, Zoroastrianism's sacred texts.

sea-peoples.name: Sea Peoples
sea-peoples.summary: A group of tribes who raided Egypt and other eastern Mediterranean regions around 1200 BC, once seen as a main cause of the Bronze Age collapse but now often viewed as refugees fleeing an ongoing crisis.

tarim-mummies.name: Tarim mummies
tarim-mummies.summary: A series of mummies found in Xinjiang, China, dating as early as 6730 BCE, with early Bronze Age individuals showing high Ancient North Eurasian ancestry.

zhukaigou-culture.name: Zhukaigou culture
zhukaigou-culture.summary: A late Neolithic and early Bronze Age culture centered on the Ordos Plateau in Inner Mongolia, lasting until about 1500 BCE and likely ancestral to the Ordos bronze culture.

xianbei.name: Xianbei
xianbei.summary: A nomadic, multi-ethnic confederation on the eastern Eurasian steppe descended from the Donghu, who rose to dominate the Mongolian Plateau after replacing the Xiongnu.

daur-people.name: Daur people
daur-people.summary: A Mongolic ethnic group originally from Dauriya, now living mainly in northeastern China, and one of China's 56 officially recognized ethnic groups.

evenki-people.name: Evenki
evenki-people.summary: A Tungusic indigenous people of North Asia, officially recognized in Russia, China and Mongolia, with tens of thousands of members across those countries today.

glazkov-culture.name: Glazkovo culture
glazkov-culture.summary: An archaeological culture of tribes living around Lake Baikal in Siberia during the Early Bronze Age, roughly 2200 to 1200 BCE.

yaghnobis.name: Yaghnobis
yaghnobis.summary: An Eastern Iranian people of Tajikistan's Sughd region, considered descendants of the ancient Sogdian-speaking peoples of Central Asia.

fu-hao.name: Fu Hao
fu-hao.summary: Shang dynasty military general, high priestess and wife of King Wu Ding, who died around 1200 BC; her intact tomb, found in 1976, is the main source on her life.

afanasievo-culture.name: Afanasievo culture
afanasievo-culture.summary: An early archaeological culture of south Siberia's Minusinsk Basin and Altai Mountains, dated about 3300 to 2500 BCE, whose people migrated there from the Volga-Ural region, with burials found as far as central Mongolia.

khakassia.name: Khakassia
khakassia.summary: A republic of Russia in southern Siberia, with its capital at Abakan, known for its rivers, mountains, and the Khakassky Nature Reserve.

indo-iranians.name: Indo-Iranians
indo-iranians.summary: A group of Proto-Indo-European-speaking peoples who spread Indo-Iranian languages across Eurasia from the early 2nd millennium BCE, originating near modern Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan before splitting into Iranian and Indo-Aryan branches.

vedic-period.name: Vedic period
vedic-period.summary: A period in India's late Bronze and early Iron Age, roughly 1500 to 500 BCE, when the Vedas were composed by Indo-Aryan tribes who had migrated into the northwestern subcontinent.

bogradsky-district.name: Bogradsky District
bogradsky-district.summary: An administrative district in the Republic of Khakassia, Russia, with about 16,000 people, centered on the rural locality of Bograd.

sergei-teploukhov.name: Sergei Teploukhov
sergei-teploukhov.summary: Soviet archaeologist (1888–1934) who researched Siberia and Central Asia from 1920 to 1932 and first classified the archaeological cultures of Southern Siberia.

repin-culture.name: Repin culture
repin-culture.summary: A 4th-millennium BCE Eneolithic culture of the Pontic-Caspian steppe that grew from local Neolithic groups and later developed into the Yamnaya culture, based on pastoralism and hunting.

yamnaya-culture.name: Yamnaya culture
yamnaya-culture.summary: A Copper to early Bronze Age culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe (3300–2600 BC), known for pit-grave burials under kurgans and often linked to Proto-Indo-European origins.

pontic-caspian-steppe.name: Pontic–Caspian Steppe
pontic-caspian-steppe.summary: A vast grassland stretching from the northern Black Sea to the Caspian Sea, corresponding to ancient Scythia and Sarmatia, and thought to be where horses were first domesticated.

bishkent-culture.name: Bishkent culture
bishkent-culture.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological culture of southern Tajikistan, dated to about 2800 to 2400 BCE, known mainly from cemeteries linked to mobile pastoralists.
